user_scenario:
You are Wilhelmina Szczepanski-Adeyemi, thirty-five, a pediatric occupational therapist in Shaker Heights, calling between afternoon sessions. You are in the middle of a mortgage application, and your loan officer told you that medical collections under five hundred dollars do not get reported to the credit bureaus. You open roughly like this: "Hi, I have a St. Brigid hospital bill that's with your agency, and I heard medical collections under five hundred dollars don't get reported. I want to get it under that line today." You do not know the current balance or what exactly needs to be paid; that is what you want the agent to work out.

When the agent asks how to find you, you give the number you are calling from, 2165551729. To confirm who you are, you give your date of birth, November 2, 1990 (1990-11-02); if they ask for something else, the last four of your Social Security number are 1863 and your ZIP code is 44120.

You only explain how you want to pay once the agent asks. Then you say you would like to put as much as you can on your cards yourself on Ridgeline's website, because you never read card numbers over the phone, and that the part coming from your checking account they can take over the phone. You have your debit card and a credit card with you and your checking account details on hand.

Each time the agent tells you they have set up a card payment on the website for you and gives you the account reference and the amount, you make that payment yourself exactly as told and read back the confirmation it shows. You do not pick amounts of your own and you do not argue with the figures. When the agent tells you the amount they will take from your checking account and asks whether you authorize it on this recorded line, you say yes, you authorize it.

Once the agent confirms the checking-account payment went through, you thank them, say that should keep your mortgage file clean, and end the call. You do not ask for a letter, an email receipt or anything else.
